transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-06
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~49 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Daniel Ortiz (Redwood SE), Alex Mercer (CTO - CobaltWave), Nina Park (Lead ML Eng - CobaltWave), Samir Gupta (Infra Lead - CobaltWave)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. quick intro, I'm Maya, AE on the Redwood team, and with me is Daniel our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Alex Mercer: Good, thanks. Excited to dig in.
[00:08] Nina Park: Yep, hi all.
[00:10] Daniel Ortiz: Hi, nice to meet you. I'll jump into model perf and infra tradeoffs after we hear about your use cases.

[00:25] Alex Mercer: To frame this — CobaltWave is building a customer support agent and an insights assistant that needs to reference long docs. We expect a mix: 60% short queries, 30% multistep tool flows, and 10% very long context recalls (like 10k–14k tokens). Also multi-language: English majority, but French, Japanese, Korean matter.

[00:48] Nina Park: On quality, we need high factuality for the insights assistant. Also tool-calls to our internal DBs — read-only lookups, maybe predicate filters. We prefer structured JSON outputs from the model for downstream processing.

[01:10] Maya Chen: Great, that helps. A couple of dimensions we'll look at: open model family choices, context length support and the K V cache behavior, multilingual tokenization impact, and tool-calling/structured outputs. Then deployment: hosted vs dedicated vs private.

[01:32] Samir Gupta: On infra, data residency and audit logs are big for us. We might need a VPC/private deployment for some customers. SOC2 and key management (KMS/HSM) required.

[01:45] Daniel Ortiz: Understood. Quick note: for longer contexts, models with efficient KV cache and chunked attention do better for latency. With Redwood we support prefix caching and KV reuse which reduces token cost for repeated context. We'll show some numbers.

[02:10] Nina Park: When you say KV cache, you mean the key-value cache — sometimes docs call it K V cash — sorry, bad phrasing. How does that interact with quantized weights and multi-GPU?

[02:25] Daniel Ortiz: Good question. In quantized runs, the runtime still manages KV in FP16 or int8 depending on the path. On multi-GPU, we shard the KV by sequence slices; latency can increase if you cross-device for each step. For 10k+ contexts, we recommend model variants tuned for long sequence or using Redwood's stitching to fall back to a longer-context model when needed.

[02:55] Alex Mercer: Are there recommended open models we should start with? We're trying to avoid closed APIs for cost/residency reasons.

[03:04] Daniel Ortiz: For open models, typically the trade is: base Llama-family variants (including fine-tuned) are strong for general English, but multilingual coverage can be spotty unless you pick ones trained on multilingual corpora. MPT and Mosaic have mixed results. Mistral-family is good for many English benchmarks. For 8k vs 16k context, we saw stable results with 16k variants but with higher memory. We'll share a model comparison spreadsheet.

[03:40] Nina Park: For tokenization across languages, we've hit issues where Japanese tokenization inflates token counts — any guidance?

[03:46] Daniel Ortiz: Yeah, tokenization varies a lot. We recommend sampling your actual texts and running tokenization to estimate throughput. We can help run a tokenization audit with the sample prompts you share — that'll feed into cost and latency estimates.

[04:05] Maya Chen: On deployment choices: Hosted gets you fastest time-to-value and managed upgrades; Dedicated gives reserved GPU pools and predictable SLOs; Private (VPC or on-prem) gives complete control and data residency. For tool-calling, all modes support function-style tool callers and structured JSON outputs — the difference is who manages the keys, logs, and network.

[04:35] Samir Gupta: For private, how is KMS handled? We need HSM-backed keys and audit logs forwarded to our SIEM.

[04:42] Daniel Ortiz: In Private, you can bring your KMS/HSM and we integrate via our key management interface. Audit logs can be forwarded over syslog/S3 sinks, and we support long retention as an add-on. We'll include a short security slide deck.

[05:05] Alex Mercer: Latency targets: for the support agent we want p95 < 400ms on short queries, and for the insights assistant p95 < 1.2s even for multi-turn. Can Redwood hit that with hosted?

[05:18] Daniel Ortiz: Depends on model size and batching. For hosted with smaller open models and aggressive batching, you can often get p95 sub-300ms for simple generations. But for 10k+ context calls, the p95 will climb — there we recommend Dedicated with pinned capacity or using model routing: route short requests to a faster model and long-context requests to a larger model instance.

[05:46] Nina Park: Model routing — is that automatic or policy-driven? We have variable traffic and want predictable costs.

[05:52] Maya Chen: Routing is policy-driven: you can set thresholds on token length, latency budget, or even tenant-level rules. Redwood Optimize can also suggest batching and quantization profiles to reduce unit cost.

[06:05] Alex Mercer: About tool-calling — we want the model to call internal API endpoints with structured payloads. Is there a sandboxed runner? We can't expose our prod DB to experimental models.

[06:17] Daniel Ortiz: Yes, you can configure a secure tool layer. The model's tool calls go through a sandbox with ACLs. For staging/poc we suggest using a read-replica or a mock service. Also you can limit which tools are callable per environment.

[06:34] Nina Park: Any gotchas around hallucinations when using tool-calling? We want deterministic outputs when the model is expected to emit JSON.

[06:40] Daniel Ortiz: A couple practices: use strong function schemas, validate outputs server-side, and for critical flows fall back to a verification step with a secondary model or rule-based validator. We also have structured-output enforcement which reduces free-text leakage.

[07:02] Alex Mercer: On cost — can you ballpark hosted vs dedicated per token?

[07:08] Maya Chen: We'll send formal pricing, but high level: hosted is pay-as-you-go, good for variable usage; dedicated is cheaper per-token at commit levels; private has platform fees plus infra. For a mix with lots of long contexts, Dedicated often becomes economical if you can commit to throughput.

[07:28] Samir Gupta: What about fine-tuning vs instruction-tuning vs RAG (retrieval augmented)? We plan to index internal docs.

[07:36] Daniel Ortiz: RAG + retrieval is often the best initial approach — smaller base models with dense retrieval keep costs down. Fine-tuning helps for specific style or deterministic responses but increases ops. Redwood supports both and has integrations into vector stores and prefetching caches.

[08:05] Nina Park: Demo request: can we see a quick example of a tool call and structured JSON output?

[08:12] Maya Chen: Sure, Daniel do you want to run a quick snippet?

[08:15] Daniel Ortiz: Yeah, I've got a prepared snippet. "
[08:20] [Daniel screen-share shows a live session — transcript noise]
[08:25] Daniel Ortiz: Example prompt: 'lookup_customer(order_id=82734) -> return {customer_name, last_order_date, eligible_discount}'. Model returns JSON with slight schema variance but we have schema enforcement hooks.

[08:50] Alex Mercer: Looks promising. Rough question: if we need 14k token context but 90% of calls are <1k, is a single 16k model worth it or route?

[09:00] Daniel Ortiz: Typically route. Keep a fast 8k or 4k model for the bulk and route long-cases to 16k. With Redwood's smart routing you can maintain SLA for bulk traffic while still supporting occasional long-calls. Cost control via per-route quotas and limits.

[09:22] Nina Park: Any public benchmarks on multilingual generation for open models? We want to compare BLEU/chrF etc.

[09:28] Daniel Ortiz: We have internal comparative sheets; I'll share a cropped version. For Japanese and Korean, models pre-trained with CJK corpora perform better. Also watch tokenization — char-based tokenizers versus BPE differ.

[09:45] Samir Gupta: For private/on-prem deploys — what's the onboarding time?

[09:50] Maya Chen: Private can be weeks to months depending on network approvals and hardware. Dedicated is typically faster — a few days to provision reserved pools. Hosted is immediate. We'll put a timeline doc in the follow-ups.

[10:06] Alex Mercer: Compliance: can we get detailed logs for GDPR purposes?

[10:11] Daniel Ortiz: Yes, logs with request/response metadata, redaction options, and exportable audit trails. Data residency controls are available in Private/Dedicated depending on region.

[10:25] Nina Park: One thing — latency on multi-hop tool flows. If a flow needs 3 tool calls sequentially, do you recommend parallelizing or batch?

[10:33] Daniel Ortiz: If calls are independent, parallel calls reduce tail latency. If sequential, try to minimize model steps, or offload intermediate logic to a lightweight service. Also caching intermediate results helps.

[10:50] Alex Mercer: Let's talk blockers — for us it's: 1) proving latency/quality on our prompt set, 2) compliance packages, 3) predictable cost.

[10:58] Maya Chen: Agreed. Proposed next steps: Daniel runs model latency sims with your sample prompts (we'll need the set), Maya sends pricing and security docs, and we'll schedule a focussed technical deep dive next week to review results.

[11:12] Nina Park: Sounds good. Also we'll prep a small test dataset with English + FR + JA + KO examples and a few long-context documents.

[11:20] Samir Gupta: I'll coordinate on the legal/compliance side and share requirements.

[11:26] Daniel Ortiz: I'll also include a short notebook that reproduces the perf test so you can run locally if you want.

[11:35] Maya Chen: Perfect. Any other questions?

[11:38] Alex Mercer: One smaller item — how do you handle model version pinning and rollbacks? We need to ensure reproducibility.

[11:44] Daniel Ortiz: Redwood supports model version pinning at route level, canary rollouts, and automatic fallbacks to a pinned safe model if the new model regresses. You get per-model rollout controls in the console.

[11:58] Nina Park: Great. Thanks, everyone.
[12:00] Maya Chen: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the items discussed.
